candidates: When modifying `flow.jison` or its companion JS modules, remove any grammar productions, token definitions, and token-list rules (e.g., orphaned `graphCodeTokens`, unused `alphaNumStatement`) that are no longer referenced by any other production, and delete corresponding dead helper code in the associated JS files. Unreferenced jison symbols accumulate silently and create maintenance debt; verify with a grep or jison linting pass that no symbol is defined but unused.

In jison grammar rule actions, prefer named semantic-value aliases (`$symbolName` built-in, or explicit label aliases via `symbol[alias]` syntax) over positional `$1`/`$2` references. Named aliases prevent off-by-one errors when alternatives are reordered or new tokens are inserted, and make the rule body self-documenting without requiring readers to count token positions.

Whenever a grammar production substitutes one non-terminal for a broader one (e.g., replacing `alphaNum` with `idString`), explicitly verify whether the substitution intentionally widens the set of accepted inputs. Add test cases that both confirm the newly-accepted forms and assert that previously-rejected forms still fail, so the intended grammar boundary is clearly documented and does not silently regress.

Mermaid diagram syntax changes must not break previously-valid diagram source. Before merging any grammar change, add regression tests for edge cases that were previously valid (e.g., trailing backslash in a quoted label `["dir\"]`, special characters at string boundaries) to verify that old diagrams continue to parse correctly and produce the same output. When a conflict arises between a new feature and backward compatibility, the old behavior must be preserved.

When grammar changes affect which escape sequences or special characters are valid inside node or edge labels, update both `packages/mermaid/src/docs/syntax/flowchart.md` and `docs/syntax/flowchart.md` to accurately reflect the current grammar: remove examples that no longer work, do not introduce examples for forms that have not been verified, and keep the two copies consistent with each other.

When flowchart parser tests exercise the same assertion body across multiple shapes, edge types, or token categories, use `it.each` or a plain JS array iteration (`forEach`/`map` over a data-table) rather than duplicating the test body for each case. This reduces file size, makes the coverage intent explicit, and makes adding new cases trivial.

For any parser change involving reserved keywords appearing inside node identifiers, add explicit tests for keywords as id prefixes, suffixes, and mid-string infixes separated by each permitted punctuation character (e.g., `_keyword`, `keyword_`, `a-keyword-b`, `a.keyword.b`). Clearly separate the cases that should parse successfully from those that should throw, so the exact language boundary is documented and cannot silently regress.

In `flow.jison`, keep shape-start/shape-end lexer token rules (e.g., `STADIUMSTART`, `SUBROUTINESTART`, `CYLINDERSTART`) decoupled from text-content state management. Handle quoted and unquoted text within the `text` grammar production (or a dedicated `string` production) rather than embedding `pushState`/`popState` calls inside the lexer rules that emit shape-start tokens. Mixing these concerns produces lexer rules whose entry state does not match their intended exit condition, causing self-contradictory lexer state machine behavior.
